descripcion: At B2 the key distinction is between defining relative clauses (essential to identify what's being talked about) and non-defining ones (extra information, set off by commas). Getting the commas right changes the meaning, not just the punctuation.

filas: The man who called is my brother.
My brother, who called earlier, is on his way.
The book that I read / The book, which I loved,

ejemplos.texto: The man who called earlier is my brother.
My brother, who lives in Berlin, is visiting next week.
The report that we discussed yesterday has been approved.

notas: In a non-defining clause, removing it doesn't change who or what is being talked about — it only adds extra detail.
That cannot be used in a non-defining clause: my brother, that lives in Berlin is not standard English.
Whose works for both people and things to show possession: the company whose logo we redesigned.

es.en: Spanish distinguishes restrictive and explanatory clauses less visibly, and «que» is used for almost everything. Spanish speakers tend to forget the commas around English non-defining clauses, unintentionally changing the meaning of the sentence.
es.es: El español distingue de forma menos visible entre relativas restrictivas y explicativas, y usa «que» para casi todo. Los hispanohablantes tienden a olvidar las comas en las non-defining clauses inglesas, cambiando sin querer el significado.

de.en: German puts commas around every relative clause, defining or not. German speakers therefore add commas to defining clauses as well, which in English turns them into non-defining ones and changes the meaning (The students, who passed, received a certificate).
de.de: Im Deutschen stehen Kommas um jeden Relativsatz, egal ob bestimmend oder nicht. Deutschsprachige setzen deshalb auch bei «defining relative clauses» Kommas; im Englischen werden sie dadurch zu «non-defining clauses» und die Bedeutung ändert sich («The students, who passed, received a certificate»).

it.en: Italian also uses commas to separate non-defining clauses, so the principle is familiar. The difficulty is the pronoun: Italian «che» covers both types, which leads to that in non-defining clauses (my brother, that lives in Rome) instead of who or which.
it.it: L'italiano usa anch'esso le virgole per separare le relative non restrittive, quindi il principio è familiare. La difficoltà sta nel pronome: «che» copre entrambi i tipi e può portare a «that» nelle non-defining clauses («my brother, that lives in Rome») invece di «who» o «which».

fr.en: French also marks non-defining clauses with commas, so the principle is familiar. The difficulty is the pronoun: French «qui» is used for people and things alike, so French speakers need to learn when English uses who, which or that.
fr.fr: Le français marque aussi les relatives non déterminatives avec des virgules, donc le principe est familier. La difficulté vient du pronom : «qui» s'utilise pour les personnes et les choses, et il faut apprendre quand l'anglais emploie «who», «which» ou «that».

pt.en: Portuguese grammar explicitly distinguishes restrictive and explanatory relative clauses and marks the latter with commas, so the principle transfers well. The difficulty is the pronoun: «que» covers both types, which leads to that in non-defining clauses (my sister, that lives in Porto).
pt.pt: A gramática do português distingue explicitamente orações relativas restritivas e explicativas e marca estas últimas com vírgulas, então o princípio se transfere bem. A dificuldade está no pronome: «que» cobre os dois tipos e pode levar a «that» em non-defining clauses («my sister, that lives in Porto»).

errores: Missing commas around a non-defining clause, which changes the meaning.
Using that in a non-defining clause.
Confusing who and which for people versus things.

redemittel.funcion: non-defining, extra info about a person
non-defining, extra info about a thing

autochequeo: Are commas present around every non-defining clause?
Is that avoided in non-defining clauses?
Is who used for people and which for things?
Does removing the clause change the meaning (defining) or just remove detail (non-defining)?
Have I used both a defining and a non-defining clause?
promptCorreccion: Focus only on defining and non-defining relative clauses. Check the commas around non-defining clauses and the choice between that and which. Do not rewrite the text at all, just mark the issues.

es: «*lo que*» rendered as *what* in a sentential relative: *He came late, what annoyed me* instead of *which annoyed me*.
de: «*alles, was*» rendered as *everything what* instead of *everything that*.
it: «*il che*» rendered as *what*: *He came late, what annoyed me* instead of *which annoyed me*.
fr: «*qui*» rendered as *who* for things, since it covers both: *the car who broke down* instead of *which* or *that*.
pt: *que* rendered as *which* for people: *the doctor which saw me* instead of *who*.
